content: 1. High-level hand hygiene performance in hospital units or wards is influenced by several factors, including accessibility to hand rubs, the presence of role models, a personal sense of responsibility, and emotional involvement. These factors can act as barriers to compliance with hand hygiene protocols. 2. Nine studies have examined the role and effectiveness of multimodal strategies in reducing catheter-related and central line-associated bloodstream infections. Eight of these were quantitative studies conducted in intensive care units, while one was a qualitative study. 3. Guidelines on the core components of infection prevention and control (IPC) programs at the national and acute healthcare facility levels have identified factors influencing behavioral change in the context of peripheral venous line use. All intervention studies employed multimodal approaches, which included the use of bundles or comprehensive procedures promoted at various levels. 4. Key elements of these multimodal strategies included senior management commitment and support, training, identification of champions or leads, and the provision of additional materials and equipment. 5. Three studies focused on catheter insertion, three addressed both catheter insertion and maintenance, and one focused on catheter care. All eight quantitative studies demonstrated a reduction in central line-associated bloodstream infection rates. 6. Four studies provided data on process indicators, and three studies addressed ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). These studies showed that multimodal prevention strategies are effective in reducing VAP rates, particularly when developed by multidisciplinary task forces, closely monitored, and supported by structured business plans and strong educational components for frontline healthcare workers. 7. In three studies, multimodal strategies were associated with overall reductions in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and Clostridioides difficile infections. MRSA infection rates were reduced through bundle-based strategies, with one study employing positive deviance principles to achieve culture change and make infection control a shared responsibility among all stakeholders. 8. Most of the included studies were conducted in high-income or upper-middle-income countries. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) assessed the overall quality of evidence as low due to medium to high risk of bias and varied study designs outside the recommended EPOC (Effective Practice and Organisation of Care) framework. 9. An additional 91 studies, including non-controlled before-after studies, non-controlled cohort trials, and one case-control study, were retrieved. Although these did not meet EPOC criteria, they provided further support for implementing IPC activities using multimodal strategies. 10. In 27 studies, multimodal strategies were shown to improve hand hygiene compliance. These strategies, which catalyzed education, system change, surveillance, and feedback, were associated with reductions in catheter-related bloodstream infections, MRSA, catheter-associated urinary tract infections, VAP, and central line-associated bloodstream infections. 11. One study demonstrated that a practice development framework, involving multidisciplinary teams, clinical assessments, practice checklists, guideline development, and education, was associated with a decrease in catheter-related bloodstream infections. 12. Bundles, whether used as standalone interventions or as part of multimodal strategies, were associated with decreased rates of central line-associated bloodstream infections, VAP, surgical site infections (SSI), catheter-associated urinary tract infections, and MRSA. 13. The GDG emphasized the importance of patient involvement in establishing or strengthening the safety climate within the context of multimodal strategies. This approach requires local adaptation and consideration of cultural specifics, social dynamics, and literacy levels. 14. The GDG recommended that national IPC programs coordinate and facilitate the implementation of IPC activities through multimodal strategies at a nationwide or sub-national level. This recommendation is based on evidence showing reductions in central line-associated bloodstream infections, MRSA infections, and increased hand hygiene compliance. 15. The GDG acknowledged that while the quality of evidence was low, the strength of the recommendation should be strong due to the innovative and effective nature of multimodal strategies in reducing healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and improving patient safety. 16. The GDG highlighted the need for further research to determine the most effective elements of multimodal strategies and to identify the key staff members driving these interventions. Qualitative research is also needed to understand the factors facilitating success and the barriers to implementation. 17. The GDG noted that successful multimodal interventions should be associated with cross-organizational culture change, as effective IPC reflects quality care, a positive organizational culture, and an enhanced patient safety climate. 18. National-level support for IPC programs, including policies, regulations, and tools, is essential for effective central coordination. The GDG emphasized the importance of country-specific adaptation of implementation strategies and the feedback of results to key stakeholders. 19. Lessons from national and sub-national hand hygiene campaigns suggest that financial and human resources are critical for the success of nationally coordinated approaches. The use of care bundles has become common in recent years as part of national evidence-based improvement programs. 20. The GDG concluded that multimodal strategies are an effective approach not only to reduce HAIs but also to achieve broader patient safety improvements.
